title: NAVTEX and Maritime Safety Information
description: Test your understanding of NAVTEX, Maritime Safety Information, message identification, receiver configuration and practical bridge procedures.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of NAVTEX onboard a ship?
options: To transmit routine operational reports from the ship to the company
To automatically receive Maritime Safety Information relevant to coastal navigation
To provide voice communication between ships and coastal stations
To replace the vessel's radar and electronic chart systems
questions.explanation: NAVTEX automatically receives Maritime Safety Information such as navigational warnings, meteorological warnings and forecasts, and search and rescue information.

questions.question: Which frequency is used for the international NAVTEX service in English?
options: 2182 kHz
490 kHz
518 kHz
questions.explanation: The international NAVTEX service broadcasts Maritime Safety Information in English on 518 kHz.

questions.question: Which type of information would normally be received through NAVTEX?
options: Crew payroll information
Navigational and meteorological warnings
Cargo invoices and charter-party instructions
Engine performance reports
questions.explanation: NAVTEX distributes Maritime Safety Information, including navigational warnings, meteorological information and urgent safety-related messages.

questions.question: Why can a NAVTEX receiver operate without continuous manual monitoring?
options: It automatically selects and receives messages according to programmed stations and subjects
It receives information only when the bridge team activates a distress alarm
It communicates directly with the vessel's radar
It automatically calls the nearest coastal station by voice
questions.explanation: NAVTEX is designed for automatic reception. The receiver uses message identification characters to process information from selected stations and subjects.

questions.question: What does the NAVTEX receiver primarily provide to the bridge team?
options: Long-range voice communication with port authorities
Automatic coastal Maritime Safety Information
Continuous identification of nearby vessels
Electronic position fixing
questions.explanation: NAVTEX provides automatically received Maritime Safety Information for vessels operating within the coverage of NAVTEX coast stations.

questions.question: What does the B1 character in a NAVTEX message identify?
options: The transmitting coastal station
The subject category of the message
The message sequence number
The language used in the message
questions.explanation: The B1 character identifies the NAVTEX transmitting station.

questions.question: What is represented by the B2 character in a NAVTEX message identity?
options: The year in which the message was transmitted
The transmitting station's geographical position
The subject or type of Maritime Safety Information
The vessel category for which the message applies
questions.explanation: The B2 character identifies the message subject, such as navigational warnings, meteorological warnings or search and rescue information.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the B3 and B4 characters?
options: They identify the receiving vessel
They form the two-digit message serial number
They specify the transmission frequency
They indicate the message's geographical coordinates
questions.explanation: B3 and B4 form the NAVTEX message number, which helps the receiver identify messages and avoid unnecessary repetition.

questions.question: Why are NAVTEX coast stations assigned scheduled transmission periods?
options: To allow several stations to share the same frequency without excessive interference
To ensure all stations transmit at the same time
To limit reception to daylight hours
To allow ships to transmit replies between broadcasts
questions.explanation: NAVTEX stations use coordinated time slots so that multiple stations can share the frequency while minimizing mutual interference.

questions.question: What is the usual role of 490 kHz in NAVTEX services?
options: International Maritime Safety Information transmitted only in English
National NAVTEX broadcasts, often using a national language
Voice distress communication between ships
Automatic transmission of a ship's position
questions.explanation: 490 kHz is used for national NAVTEX services and may carry information in a national language.

questions.question: A vessel is approaching a new coastal area, but the NAVTEX receiver is configured only for stations near the previous port. What is the main risk?
options: The receiver may miss relevant warnings from stations covering the vessel's new route
The receiver will automatically transmit a false distress alert
The ship's GPS position will become inaccurate
The receiver will erase all previously received messages
questions.explanation: The bridge team must ensure that stations relevant to the intended route are selected. Otherwise, important Maritime Safety Information may not be received.

questions.question: A received NAVTEX message begins with the identity code KA27. What does the letter K indicate?
options: The message is intended only for cargo vessels
The transmitting station identity
The message was transmitted on 490 kHz
The warning expires in one day
questions.explanation: The first character after the message header is the B1 character, which identifies the transmitting NAVTEX station.

questions.question: In the NAVTEX identity KA27, what does the letter A indicate?
options: A navigational warning
A message transmitted in English
The first transmission of the day
An acknowledgement request
questions.explanation: Subject indicator A is used for navigational warnings.

questions.question: A previously received warning is broadcast again with the same B1, B2, B3 and B4 identity. Why may the receiver reject the repeated transmission?
options: The receiver recognizes that the message identity has already been received
NAVTEX receivers accept only one message from each station per voyage
Repeated warnings are automatically considered cancelled
The receiver cannot receive the same subject twice
questions.explanation: The complete message identity allows the receiver to recognize previously received messages and avoid repeatedly printing or displaying the same information.

questions.question: A navigational warning has been received with several corrupted or missing sections. What should the officer of the watch do?
options: Ignore the message because incomplete NAVTEX messages have no operational value
Assess its relevance and obtain the complete warning through another appropriate source
Assume that the missing text contains no safety-critical information
Delete the message and wait for the next scheduled voyage
questions.explanation: An incomplete warning may still indicate a significant hazard. The officer should determine its relevance and seek a complete version through another available MSI source.

questions.question: A vessel receives a search and rescue message concerning persons in distress near its route. What is the most appropriate bridge response?
options: Delete the message because NAVTEX information is advisory only
Record the message but take no further action unless contacted by the company
Immediately assess the vessel's position, the message and any obligations to assist
Wait until the next routine NAVTEX transmission confirms the incident
questions.explanation: Search and rescue information requires immediate assessment by the master or officer of the watch, including the vessel's ability and obligation to provide assistance.

questions.question: The bridge team has deselected meteorological warnings because too many routine messages were being received. What is the principal concern?
options: The receiver may no longer display information essential to safe route planning
The NAVTEX transmitter may suspend broadcasts to the vessel
The vessel's weather-routing service will automatically terminate
The receiver will switch from 518 kHz to VHF
questions.explanation: Excessive filtering may prevent the bridge team from receiving safety-critical information. Receiver settings should reflect the vessel's operational area and information needs.

questions.question: Why should the officer of the watch check both the station identity and the geographical content of a NAVTEX warning?
options: A message received from a selected station is not necessarily relevant to the vessel's route
Station identities determine whether COLREG applies
The geographical content controls the receiver's transmission power
Every message from a nearby station must be entered in the Oil Record Book
questions.explanation: NAVTEX coverage areas can overlap, and a station may transmit warnings for a broad region. The bridge team must assess the actual geographical relevance of each message.

questions.question: A NAVTEX receiver has not received any scheduled broadcasts while nearby vessels report normal reception. Which action is most appropriate first?
options: Verify the receiver frequency, station selections, antenna condition and equipment status
Transmit a distress alert to the coastal station
Change the vessel's assigned sea area
Disable all message subject filters permanently
questions.explanation: The bridge team should systematically check receiver configuration, selected stations, antenna connections, power supply and fault indications.

questions.question: A navigational warning concerns an unlit buoy directly on the vessel's planned route. What is the best use of the NAVTEX information?
options: Retain it only as evidence that the receiver is operational
Use it to review the passage plan, brief the bridge team and apply appropriate navigational precautions
Wait for the warning to appear automatically on the radar
Forward it to the engine room without changing the passage plan
questions.explanation: Relevant NAVTEX warnings must be incorporated into voyage planning and bridge operations, including route review, chart-related precautions and watchkeeper briefings.
